content: For instance, if tuberculosis (TB) patients are to be categorized based on their country of origin, every patient must be asked to provide this information. Completed clinical information forms should be sent to the coordination team, while the original forms are retained at the diagnostic center. Ensuring the accuracy of patient classification, particularly regarding their history of TB treatment (new versus previously treated), is critical for reliable data analysis and interpretation. Special efforts must be made during surveys to verify the reliability of clinical data. This includes incorporating specific questions in clinical forms to accurately capture treatment history, carefully reviewing collected forms for deficiencies, and regularly assessing the reliability of recorded information. Re-interviewing patients, especially a representative sample (e.g., 10%), can help verify treatment histories. All patients with rifampicin resistance, particularly new patients, should also be re-interviewed. Verification of treatment history is especially important in settings where incentives for detecting new patients or other factors may encourage falsification of treatment history. Patients may be more willing to provide accurate treatment details once they begin feeling better after starting treatment. It is often observed that surveys record a higher proportion of previously treated cases compared to routine programmatic data. This discrepancy may result from the more comprehensive treatment history documentation in surveys, which reduces patient misclassification. Proper collection, processing, and rapid transportation of sputum samples to participating laboratories are crucial for obtaining accurate and reliable results. The number of samples required depends on the testing methods used. Health care workers must be well-trained to instruct patients on collecting high-quality sputum samples. Since aerosols containing Mycobacterium tuberculosis can be generated during sputum production, patients should produce sputum (not saliva) in open-air environments or specially designed collection rooms with proper ventilation or ultraviolet irradiation to minimize the risk of transmission. Sputum collection should not occur in confined spaces like laboratory rooms or toilets. Samples must be handled with care, using rigid, watertight containers with wide-mouthed screw tops to prevent leakage and contamination. Containers should be packed with absorbent material to manage accidental leakage. Before transport, sputum samples should be stored in a cool place, preferably refrigerated at +4°C. Cool boxes should be used for transportation to laboratories. If delays in transportation exceeding 3–4 days are anticipated, 1% cetylpyridinium chloride (CPC) should be added to the sputum to preserve it. However, CPC-treated samples should not be refrigerated, as low temperatures may cause crystallization and inactivation. CPC-treated sputum can only be cultured on egg-based media, not liquid or agar media. Molecular tests like Xpert MTB/RIF and line probe assays yield reliable results with CPC-treated sputum, which can be tested up to one month after collection if stored at ambient temperature. Each sputum container must be labeled with the patient’s unique survey identification number (not on the lid), and standard laboratory forms should accompany the samples during shipment. Laboratory methods must adhere to the diagnostic testing algorithm established during survey planning. For culture-based surveys, sputum decontamination is performed to destroy non-mycobacterial bacteria and homogenize the sample. The preferred technique globally is the Petroff method, which uses sodium hydroxide (NaOH) at a final concentration of up to 2%. If CPC was used for transport, NaOH decontamination should only be applied if the delay from collection to processing exceeds one week, with a reduced contact time of 5–10 minutes. For liquid culture, the NaLC-NaOH method is recommended. Sputum specimens should be refrigerated at +4°C until processed, except for CPC-treated samples, which should not be refrigerated. All positive cultures should be stored in a deep freezer at -20°C or lower until retesting is completed or the strain is excluded from further testing. The transportation of TB cultures requires strict adherence to safety regulations to mitigate risks associated with accidents or container breakage. Drug susceptibility testing (DST) should be performed on one isolate per patient using WHO-recommended methods. Laboratories must demonstrate proficiency in DST by participating in at least one round of proficiency testing with a supranational reference laboratory (SRL) before the survey. If second-line DST is unavailable in the country, it can be conducted at an SRL, provided sufficient resources are allocated to cover costs. Results should be recorded on standard laboratory forms and sent to the survey coordination team and diagnostic center. Molecular-based surveys can incorporate WHO-endorsed tests, such as Xpert MTB/RIF, which can be performed at district or sub-district levels, reducing logistical challenges. A checklist can help assess compliance with inclusion/exclusion criteria, safe sputum collection and transport, and data completeness. Any significant issues identified should be addressed promptly, and missing information should be requested from respective centers. A midterm review meeting should be held to evaluate data quality, laboratory procedures, and preliminary results. External monitoring by independent experts is also recommended. Data management aims to produce high-quality, reliable data on individual characteristics and aggregated indicators, such as the proportion of multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) cases. A database manager should oversee the development of a centrally managed database. All enrolled patients, including those with lost or contaminated samples, should be entered into the database. Barcode labels and handheld scanners are recommended to minimize transcription errors. Data analysis should include developing a flowchart to track patient outcomes and identify potential biases. Analyses should address missing data patterns, drug resistance patterns, and determinants of resistance. Specialized statistical software is required for cluster-sampled surveys to account for missing data and sampling design effects. Multiple imputation of missing values may reduce bias but should not replace the collection of high-quality data. Sampling weights may be applied to correct for variations in cluster sizes, but weights should not be used when assessing risk factors for drug resistance. Interpretation of survey results should consider potential biases, such as misclassification of treatment history or cross-contamination in laboratory processes. High proportions of drug resistance among new cases may indicate misclassification or recent transmission of resistant strains. Younger age groups provide more reliable information on recent transmission patterns. Previously treated cases are a heterogeneous group, and factors like unsupervised treatment, inadequate drug regimens, and poor-quality drugs contribute to acquired resistance. Subgroup analyses can yield targeted conclusions, but small sample sizes may limit their feasibility. Periodic surveys and trends over time should be interpreted cautiously, considering the limitations of the data.
